Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. For a witnessed-other-trauma presentation, the other threat items describe hypervigilance and startle around other people, and the triggers/memory/appraisal items do not suggest a home-intrusion or boundary-violation danger theme. Repeated door/window checking points to a specific safety behavior focused on securing the environment, which is not supported elsewhere in the selected items and does not fit the formulation well, especially given that maladaptive-strategy links are inactive.

vignette: At seventy-one, Tane, a second-generation Fijian American, stood in a grocery store aisle a decade ago when a heavy service door slammed inward with a metallic crack, immediately followed by the sharp, unrelenting wail of an infant left unattended in a shopping cart. He watched as a stranger shoved a stock clerk to the ground and vanished through the emergency exit, leaving behind a scene that refused to cohere in his mind. Even now, when Tane tries to explain what occurred, he loses the thread mid-sentence, unable to construct a clear story for himself or anyone else. Because he could not piece together a complete picture of those events, he came to believe that the institutions meant to protect the community had deliberately looked away, and that those responsible would face no accountability. This conviction that no justice would come steadily drained his capacity for feeling, leaving him emotionally numb to the routines and relationships he once valued. The inability to form a coherent memory of the attack kept his mind searching for patterns in the present, and the more he struggled to recall the event, the more acutely he felt the jolt of discomfort whenever a checkout door opened or a shopping cart rattled nearby. Those auditory cues quickly spiked his breathing at his current cashier station, and the sudden discomfort propelled him into a state of relentless hypervigilance. He began watching other people closely for signs of impending harm, his eyes tracking hands and shoulders rather than scanning the items on the conveyor belt. When a customer suddenly reached past him to grab a receipt, Tane's body startled to the movement, reacting as if he were in immediate danger. This constant state of high alert convinced him that the world was inherently unsafe, which only deepened his belief that the authorities had failed to safeguard him. His distrust of those institutions made him hyper-focused on potential threats, and the more he monitored strangers' movements, the more convinced he became that accountability was an illusion. That unresolved sense of institutional failure made the memory of the attack feel even more fragmented, pulling his attention back to the sound of latches clicking and distant cries. The inability to piece the past together kept pulling his awareness toward every slamming door and every unattended wail, while his deep-seated distrust of those in power sharpened his focus on every potential breach. The tighter his hypervigilance became, the more certain he grew that he could never trust the systems around him, and that conviction only looped back to keep his nervous system braced for the next strike. Working the morning shift meant facing the automatic doors every time a delivery truck arrived, and the metallic thud of the mechanism now served as a reliable cue that danger was near. This persistent sense of discomfort convinced him that the people entrusted with public safety had abandoned their post, reinforcing his conviction that those responsible would never answer for what he witnessed. His emotional numbness made the daily interactions at the register feel hollow, and that detachment only widened the gap between him and his wife, who asked why he had stopped sharing meals or attending neighborhood gatherings. He found himself scanning the checkout line for any sudden shift in posture, which kept him locked in a state of high alert. The more he braced for violence, the more convinced he became that the community was fundamentally unsafe, which in turn kept him hyper-focused on strangers' hands and faces. This constant monitoring made it impossible to retrieve a complete picture of the past, and the more fragmented his memories became, the more he fixated on the sound of latches clicking and distant cries. The tighter the loop grew, the more certain he felt that accountability was impossible, and that certainty only sharpened his hypervigilance, pulling him further into the present moment while the past remained a locked door. Over the past several months, this cycle has hardened into a daily routine that has strained his marriage and his work. He avoids eye contact at the checkout lane, interpreting a customer's tired posture as a precursor to violence, which keeps him locked in a loop of scanning for danger rather than processing the past. He has started leaving work early whenever the automatic doors cycle too frequently, fearing another sudden breach, and the absence of a clear narrative about what happened keeps his nervous system braced for the next strike. Last week, he finally sat down with a counselor, hoping to understand why his body still jolts at the sound of a closing door, and what he fears most is that he will never be able to piece the fragments together or trust that the world will ever be safe again.
